item.title: Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil
item.description:

Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil

Brazilian firm Estúdio 41 has completed Guaratuba House, which features exterior screens and a structural system that “explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete“.

Located in the seaside community of Prainha, which sits within the city of Guaratuba in southern Brazil, the holiday home was designed for a family to serve as “a refuge between the mountains and the sea”.

“One of their main requirements was, therefore, a strong visual connection between the interior spaces and the surrounding natural landscape,” said Estúdio 41, an architectural firm based in Curitiba.

Rectangular in plan, the 375-square-metre house has two floors. It is wrapped in folding screens made of perforated melamine panels.

The screens filter natural light and reduce solar gain on glass surfaces. When opened up, they reveal views of the scenic landscape.

“At night, the transparency and geometric patterns of the house’s skin give it the appearance of a lantern within the landscape,” the team said.

To protect against flooding, as the coastal site has been affected by storm surges in the past, the building was lifted up 70 centimeters (2.3 feet).

It has a prefabricated concrete structural system that was assembled in only six hours, with the concrete structural elements left visible.

The system consists of six columns, four beams and 20 double-tee slabs, also known as “π” (pi)-shaped slabs. The latter are pre-stressed concrete panels with a cross-section that resembles the Greek letter π.

“The project explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete,” said the team.

“The conception of a very simple and easily executable construction system reflects a concern for the realities of the local workforce,” it contniued.

“The construction technique, the modular arrangement of the structural components, and the ribs of the double-tee floor slabs are all clearly legible.”

Rooms feature artful decor and a neutral colour palette. The ground level contains an open-plan kitchen, dining area and living room, along with service areas and a guest bedroom.

The communal area opens toward a garden, and beyond it, a sheltered barbecue terrace and a swimming pool.

“The social areas were conceived as one large veranda in direct contact with the beach sand, with views of both the sea and mountains,” the team said.

The upper level contains four bedrooms, including the primary suite, and a family room. A bridge passes over the garden below and connects to a concrete terrace with sweeping views of the sea.

Other projects by Estudio 41 include a small white house in Brazil with a roof garden, and a prefabricated, teal-coloured research station in Antarctica.

item.title: Texas reveals proposal for US Space Academy in Houston
item.description:

Texas reveals proposal for US Space Academy in Houston

The Texas Space Commission has published a proposal for the newly created United States Space Academy. It would be located in Houston on a site alongside NASA‘s Johnson Space Center, which was formerly home to Mission Control.

Revealed earlier this week, the proposals show clusters of buildings arranged in a flower-like shape, with petals surrounded by water. The renders place the facility on a currently vacant site alongside the NASA facility.

The proposal was created as a response to a request for information from the American space agency, which is looking to find a permanent home for the academy.

It follows an executive order issued earlier this year by president Donald Trump that established a presidential commission to determine how the proposed NASA-led institution could be formed.

In the order, he stated that the United States Space Academy would be established with the aim of training the “next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters”.

The proposed academy would contain facilities for academic and more hands-on training.

It has received bipartisan support in Texas, with Republican senator Ted Cruz and Democrat senator-elect James Talarico issuing a joint statement in support of the bid.

“Texas has maintained a leading role in America’s human spaceflight program for decades, from training astronauts to directing missions at Johnson Space Center,” said the pair in the statement.

“The Lone Star State has developed an extensive space industry, infrastructure, and expertise. Texas is best suited to train the next generation of American space leaders and is the natural home for the U.S. Space Academy.”

According to the Texas Space Commission, the scheme was designed to align with NASA’s proposed timeline, which envisions groundbreaking commencing next year.

NASA recently announced plans for a permanent moon base, with a multi-phased plan culminating in “semi-permanent habitation models”.

Photography courtesy of Texas Space Commission

item.title: Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone
item.description:

Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone

Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro.

Named Casa Los Cobos, the home is located in Xangri-Lá on Brazil’s southern coast, and was designed to make the most of panoramic views out over the sea from the rear of the site.

Set back from the road, a series of routes both through and around the home “reveal the landscape gradually,” including a path beneath a timber canopy and via a paved veranda screened by lush plants.

“The main opportunity was the merging of two adjoining lots into a single site that extends to the rear, where the landscape opens onto the water,” Ambidestro co-founder João Pedro Crescente told Dezeen.

The ground floor of Casa Los Cobos has been given over almost entirely to a single large living, dining and kitchen space, wrapped by service spaces and bathrooms.

Full-height sliding glass doors allow this space to be opened out onto a large sheltered terrace alongside a swimming pool, with a lawn that slopes down to a nearby waterway.

“The ground floor is free of partitions: living, dining and the entertaining kitchen are integrated and turned toward the greenery, accommodating everything from a weeknight dinner to a Saturday party,” Crescente told Dezeen.

“Between the living room and the water lie, in sequence, the veranda, the garden and the pool, which wraps around the house. The eye passes through these layers before reaching the backdrop,” he added.

Both the exterior and interior have been given contrasting finishes of rough Morelo stone and white plaster and paint, with the rear terrace framed by white-painted masonry.

This is complemented internally with bespoke carpentry in pale oak, including a floating timber bar supported by a concrete column that defines one edge of the living space.

“The intention was to use natural, local materials in light, warm tones repeated inside and out, making the transition between spaces almost imperceptible,” said Crescente.

“Moledo stone clads the facades and changes in appearance from morning to late afternoon. Other natural stones continue onto the floors and wet areas,” he added.

A skylit staircase leads up to the more compartmentalised first floor of the home, which contains six en-suite bedrooms, two of which open onto a balcony overlooking the sea.

To provide both shading and privacy from the road, sliding timber shutters can be pulled down over the full-height bedroom windows.

Other homes in Brazil recently featured on Dezeen include a home in São Paolo by Studio Arthur Casas featuring dramatic overhangs and cantilevers, and a low-lying dwelling by Sabella Arquitetura that is topped by a gridded timber roof.

Photography by Gabriel Konrath

item.title: Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging profile of an influential designer with useful vocabulary and context.

Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler’s pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

Next up in Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.

Goti has experienced a remarkable rise since presenting a furniture collection made from salvaged foam insulation during the 2023 edition of Milan design week.

Her conceptual, research-led work typically explores heritage, identity and craftsmanship, resulting in playful objects and spaces that reexamine the cultural codes embedded in design.

Goti was nominated as an emerging talent to watch by American designer Wearstler, who praised how Goti “approaches ornament with the precision of an engineer and the instincts of a sculptor”.

“That refusal to treat craft and technology as opposites is going to matter more over the next 20 years,” Wearstler added.

As well as a shared love of ornament and the decorative arts, Wearstler also picked up on how Goti’s practice is informed by her background in robotics and machine learning.

“It’s amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail,” Goti told Dezeen.

It’s amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail

Goti added that she was pleased to be recognised by a leading female designer, as her creative muses are mostly women and femininity plays a major role in her own practice.

“My work is very personal so of course there are a lot of references to being a woman,” she said, adding that she draws inspiration from well-known artists and designers such as Louise Bourgeois and Faye Toogood.

Goti spoke to Dezeen from Paris, where she currently lives with her partner, French filmmaker Vincent Staropoli, having recently relocated there from New York.

She was raised in Thessaloniki and received a diploma in architecture from the local AUTh university before completing a masters degree in Integrative Technologies and Architectural Design Research at Stuttgart’s Institute of Computational Design.

The move to New York came after accepting a research position at Pratt Institute, but during the Covid pandemic Goti realised that she missed making her own work, so began experimenting with found materials.

“I really didn’t know what I wanted to do,” she recalled. “But through my research at the university and the New York design community I realised there were other people working in a similar way, which encouraged me to stick with it.”

The initial collection was followed by projects made with glass, marble and, most recently, a series of furniture pieces featuring lacquered wooden surfaces that contrast with bell-like aluminium elements.

The outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’

Goti explained that her work usually starts with research into a specific technique or a material that interests her, before she then applies her findings to the design of an object.

She said she finds this approach creatively fulfilling as it offers endless opportunities, though as someone early in her career it means there is no identifiable style associated with her work.

“I don’t usually have a form or a shape in mind when I start,” she said. “So the outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’.”

“In the long term I hope people will recognise my work because of its research-led approach,” she continued. “We need to take more time to understand other artists’ work and not judge everything based on a few images on social media.”

Decoration and ornamentation are recurring elements within Goti’s oeuvre, although she doesn’t want to be labelled as a maximalist.

“My work is sometimes very ornamental and sometimes it’s more minimal,” she added. “So there’s a gradient and the outcome is really determined by the process.”

Like many contemporary designers, Goti does not produce all of her own work, instead utilising a network of expert artisans to help bring her whimsical and deeply personal creations to life.

“I’m a very collaborative person and I think we can create better outcomes when we put our minds together with other people,” she said.

“My architecture background really helped me develop this collaborative mindset and I think one of the key things you learn as you get older is to be selective about who you work with.”

I’m a very collaborative person and I think we can create better outcomes when we put our minds together with other people

The collection she developed with Marble Sachanas (top) exemplifies this collaborative approach, applying Goti’s visionary and playful style to an ancient material sourced from a quarry close to her home town.

Goti met the company’s representatives during 2025’s Milan design week and struck up a conversation that led to them returning this year to exhibit the outcomes as part of the Alcova event.

Projects such as the marble pieces and the furniture she developed for Mexican gallery Toro Manifesto fall into the category of collectible design, which Goti pointed out is a consequence of their artisanal production rather than a conscious decision to make high-end, limited-edition objects.

“Everything nowadays is so expensive to make,” she explained. “If you want to make something that’s well-crafted you have to pay for the materials, the shipping, the labour and that causes the price to be high – it’s not the designer’s fault.”

The armchair, coffee table and sideboard were shown at the Collectible design fair in New York, but Goti said she would also be interested in working on designs that could be licensed and produced by a brand.…

Hawkins\Brown’s temporary housing for homeless families in London is a UK first

Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London, the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK.

Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.

Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.

Intending to set a benchmark for temporary family housing in the UK, Hawkins\Brown aimed to create a welcoming building that eases the stress of families facing homelessness.

“Many of the families who come here are fleeing hugely painful domestic situations,” said Hawkins\Brown partner Nick Gaskell.

“The Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre aims to make a traumatic period a little more bearable by providing a caring, calming and uplifting environment for as long as they need it.”

Designed to be in keeping with the neighbouring buildings, the exterior of the U-shaped building is lined with striped bands of orange-toned bricks and pops of pale green metal sheeting.

A secure, landscaped courtyard with play space at the centre of the building helps bring natural light into the surrounding flats.

Inside, the apartments were designed to offer higher-quality living arrangements than typical temporary housing, with tall windows, underfloor heating and open-plan kitchen, living and dining rooms.

Community and family support spaces on the ground floor of the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre include a reception, visitor breakout areas, children’s indoor play spaces, communal laundries and staff facilities.

Based on the studio’s research into dementia-friendly design, Hawkins\Brown used colour zoning, visual landmarks, accessible graphics and high-contrast colours in the centre, aiming to make the space easy to navigate for residents and visitors of all ages and abilities.

Elsewhere in London, architecture studio HTA Design recently unveiled what it says is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

In Ukraine, architecture studio Office for Future is working on plans to transform a school into temporary housing for families affected by the war in the country.

Photography by Fred Howarth

item.title: Rachel Whiteread punctures 2027 Brit Award trophy
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Unique design of a trophy with useful vocabulary, but lacks depth.

Artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for next year’s Brit Awards trophy, a silver sculpture covered in holes to “expose the interior of the statue”.

Since 1992, a different creative has been selected to design the handheld trophy for the UK music industry’s annual Brit Awards.

Essex-born Whiteread has designed the statuette for next February’s ceremony, which is her interpretation of the annual trophy depicting Britannia, a helmeted warrior that is a traditional symbol of Britain.

The result is a minimalist silver statuette cast in resin and covered in holes to draw attention to the inside of the trophy.

“I exposed the interior of the statue, as an artist would do with their music,” said Whiteread.

Whiteread then handpainted the nickel-plated trophy in a silver hue.

The artist is known for casting everyday architectural forms, such as staircases or sheds, in materials including plaster and concrete to showcase their negative space.

She explained that when designing the Brit Award, she wanted to put her own spin on the recognisable trophy.

“I saw this as a natural extension of my work – to continue to celebrate and recognise British art and creativity,” said Whiteread.

“Art and culture are under very real threat,” she continued. “So I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists, whether from music or the visual arts.”

The Brit Awards will take place on 27 February 2027 at the Populous-designed Co-op Live arena in Manchester, where the ceremony was held for the first time at the start of this year.

To mark the awards’ departure from London, where it was held consecutively before 2026, British fashion designer Matthew Williamson designed an amber trophy to reference Manchester’s worker bee city logo.

Other former trophy designers have included British architect Zaha Hadid and British-Indian artist Anish Kapoor.

item.title: Friday Five with Nick Doyle: Seeing America Through Shades of Blue
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Profile of an artist with useful vocabulary, but lacks depth.

Creative minds can seemingly turn anything into art—from household items and food to packing supplies and bottle caps. For Los Angeles-born interdisciplinary artist Nick Doyle, the material of choice is denim. Even when working in other mediums, he often gravitates toward a denim-blue palette, as in his latest exhibition, “Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found.”

Presented at Pace Prints’ New York gallery this fall, the exhibition marks Doyle’s first venture into printmaking, using graphic interpretations of everyday objects to examine American preoccupations with risk and reward, escapism, and the myth of the self-made man. The gallery will present a selection of these works at Art Basel Miami Beach 2026.

Now based in Brooklyn, Doyle earned a BFA in interdisciplinary arts from the San Francisco Art Institute and an MFA in sculpture from Hunter College, in addition to studying at Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture. He cites his discovery of denim as an artistic medium as a turning point in his career.

“I had been doing a ton of research on American history and making work exploring our relationship to nostalgia,” he recalls. “One day a fashion designer moved out of the neighboring studio and threw away a ton of stuff. I found a bolt of denim, and my brain flashed across a network of ideas I had already been considering. I intuitively knew I had stumbled across something significant.”

Represented by Perrotin and Brussels-based Stems Gallery, Doyle typically uses denim collage to explore what he calls the “underlying structures in American culture.” His practice encompasses “painting-like wall works as well as interactive installations,” he says.

Doyle’s recent exhibition, Collective Hallucinations, presented at Perrotin New York this past spring, featured wall-mounted collages and an interactive installation called “Mirror Mirror.” The denim-clad structure featured a sign reading “Psychic Readings $10 Special,” while inside, a sassy AI avatar named Ava greeted visitors. The installation marked Doyle’s first foray into AI.

In another unexpected move, he presented his corporate-themed kink bar, Human Resources, at Basel Social Club in Switzerland this June. Built from repurposed cubicles and office furniture, the installation plays with the power dynamics inherent in both corporate and kink culture.

Doyle calls his work “more of a reflection of American culture than an individualist perspective.” Reflecting on being raised Quaker, he says, “It’s a very consensus-driven community that is slow-paced and meditative. It’s culturally very counter to a fast-paced, consumer-driven way of life typical of growing up in a large American city.” The tension between these two ways of life surfaces throughout his work.

In this week’s Friday Five, we spent five minutes with Nick Doyle ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, where Pace Prints will present selections from Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found, to discuss the inspirations behind his exploration of the contradictions of American life.

The Project: Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found

As with much of Doyle’s work, his latest exhibition examines the greed, excess, and toxic masculinity of American culture, this time through bold representations of the minutiae of everyday life: a folded shirt, a necktie, a lottery ticket, a gas gauge on empty, a Coca-Cola machine. Rendered in blue tones reminiscent of denim, the imagery evokes American labor and the archetype of the self-made man.

Together, the works question the country’s deep-rooted belief in self-reliance, drawing parallels between the ideal of the independent American and today’s “America First” mentality, in which individual freedom can come at the expense of collective responsibility. A selection of these works will be on view at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 2–6, 2026.

Here, Doyle discusses his inspirations for the exhibition in his own words.

What Inspired Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found?

The Ken Burns Documentary: Country Music

“This documentary has everything: It traces the origins of country music alongside American history and is a deeply emotional story about the search for salvation and community.

“One of the musical groups featured is The Sons of the Pioneers. The title of this exhibition Lonely but Free I’ll be Found is a lyric in their song ‘Tumbling Tumbleweeds.’ Originally a poem written by Bob Nolan in the 1930s, it describes lonely cowboys adrift on the range.”

The Neon Museum in Las Vegas

“I take a lot of road trips in the Southwest. Vegas is a great access point, and one of my favorite places is the Neon Museum with a collection of old signage from the last century. There’s something about these retrofuturistic signs rotting away in the desert that I relate to. They exude a sad psychological aura of something that once served a purpose, sitting in functionless rows like a graveyard.

“I think of this body of work functioning similarly to these signs, although different in the sense that what I’m drawing attention to is an idea rather than something that can be purchased.”

The Suicide Belt

“For this show, I was considering the perspective of a man who lived in the ‘suicide belt,’ a term coined by Matt Wray in the early 2000s to describe the high-suicide-rate region of the U.S. Mountain/Intermountain West. The belt includes Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming.

“Wray describes ‘the Intermountain West as a place that is disproportionately populated by middle-aged and aging white men, single, unattached, often unemployed, with access to guns.’ I often think about suicide as a larger social symptom and connect it to broader social issues in the U.S.”
